doc.title: Keith Ingham interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Albums of Victor Young and Fred Astaire songs
summary: Ingham discusses his Fred Astaire album and why Astaire's light rhythmic singing had a jazz feel.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: Well you’ve done a lot of research, I can tell because you’ve recorded albums of Victor Young’s songs.
And Fred Astaire? Is that the music that Fred Astaire was associated with?

Yeah, I mean composers seemed to love Fred Astaire for some reason. I mean he might not be a singer, it’s not a singer’s voice per se, it’s not like Crosby, Sinatra, Perry Como has got a very good voice and everything like that, and Tony Bennett up to a point, but I mean Fred Astaire had a way, I think because he had such a great rhythmic sense, being a dancer, his delivery was very light. And he sang those Berlin songs, you know like “Putting All My Eggs In One Basket.” [scats] He had a jazz feel in his singing, as well as in his dancing. And it’s beautiful, I mean it’s so right, and elegant. And to me he had a jazz feeling. He wasn’t a jazz singer. Like what is a jazz singer quote unquote now? Who knows? Certainly not scatting and stuff. I mean but he just had a lovely lightness of touch. And they all seemed to love the way he sang their songs. So yeah, we did an album of his tunes. They’re wonderful tunes. They’re the — Gershwin wrote “Shall We Dance” and then he sings Irving Berlin, I forget the names of the damn movies now with Ginger Rogers, but it was incredible, in the 30s you know.
